title: "without fear, without hate"
last: SAT NAAM — THE NAME IS TRUTH.

lines: TWO WORDS THAT CUT THROUGH BOTH.
cards: A boss with someone's job in their hands. A bully at the bus stop. And on the other side, a grudge kept for years.
Fear and hate are strange twins: people fear those with power over them, resent those who wronged them, and between the two they can fill a whole life.
In the root verse, Guru Nanak describes God with two words that cut right through both.

teach.b: Bhau means fear. Vair means enmity, the settled hostility of an enemy. So: without fear, without hate.
Why together? Fear is what you feel toward something that could hurt you. Hate is what you feel toward something you think is against you.
A God who is one, who holds everything, has nothing outside to fear and no enemy to hate. The verse goes on: beyond time, never born, existing by itself, known by the Guru's grace.
But these two words have a life of their own, because Sikhs don't only say them about God. They take them as a picture of who a person can become.

teach.h: FRIGHTENS NO ONE, FEARS NO ONE.
teach.b: The ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, wrote a short verse describing the wise person as one who frightens no one, and is frightened by no one. Both halves matter. Fearless isn't enough if it makes you frightening.
Gentle isn't enough if it makes you afraid. So nirbhau, nirvair isn't only a description to admire from a distance.

teach.h: NOT JUST ABOUT GOD. A DIRECTION.

how: Sikhs recite the whole Mool Mantar, including nirbhau and nirvair, at the start of Japji Sahib each morning, and the phrase is often held up as an ideal for how a Sikh should live.

games.q: what's inside the line — tap the pairs.

s: nirbhau and nirvair are only said about God
Sikhs also take them as a picture of who a person can become.
the ninth Guru described the wise as frightening no one and fearing no one
a short verse by Guru Tegh Bahadur, near the end of the scripture.
the root verse ends with nirvair
it goes on: beyond time, never born, self-existent, and known by the Guru's grace.

games.q: someone powerful is pushing you around. what does nirbhau, nirvair ask of you?
o: stand your ground, and refuse to hate them.
games.why: both halves together: not afraid, and not an enemy. Guru Tegh Bahadur's verse praises the one who frightens no one and fears no one.

practice: Breathe, and name one thing you're afraid of. Then bring to mind one person you hold something against. Loosen your grip on both, only a little.
If you like, let the words go out with the breath: nirbhau, nirvair.

wordCard.voice: The Mool Mantar, line two. Nirbhau, nirvair: without fear, without hate. Said of God, and taken as a direction for a life. Eleventh word.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: nir (without) + bhau (fear); nir + vair (enmity).

carryVoice: Your line: nirbhau, nirvair. Less fear and less hate, both at once, which is harder than either alone. Day eleven.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (the Mool Mantar: Nirbhau, Nirvair, Akaal Moorat, Ajooni, Saibhang, Gur Prasad)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427 (Salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur: one who frightens no one and fears no one)
